title: Designing Under Physical & Cost Constraints
summary: Treating the speed of light and the monthly bill as design inputs, not afterthoughts — the constraints a senior engineer names before proposing a fix.

slides.markdown:
Every design has two constraints no amount of clever engineering removes: the **speed of light** (physics puts a floor on cross-region latency) and the **monthly bill** (every byte stored, replicated, and transferred costs real money). Senior engineers name these up front instead of discovering them after the design is built.

This topic treats latency and cost as design **inputs** — numbers you reason about from the start — rather than problems to patch over later.

slides.sectionTitle: The speed-of-light floor: why cross-region latency has a hard minimum
slides.markdown:
Light in fiber travels at roughly two-thirds the speed of light in a vacuum — about 200,000 km/s. A round trip between, say, US-East and Europe (~6,000 km one-way, ~12,000 km round trip) takes at least `12,000 / 200,000 ≈ 60ms`, purely from physics — before any processing, routing overhead, or queueing.

No faster CPU, no better code, and no amount of caching *at that node* fixes this: if a request genuinely must cross that distance, 60ms is the floor, not the ceiling. This is why global-latency requirements ("under 50ms worldwide") aren't purely an engineering problem — they're partly a geography problem, solved by moving computation closer to users, not by making a single distant server faster.

Lay the physical floor next to the requirement: if the product needs a 30ms p99 response but the nearest replica of the needed data is 80ms of pure network distance away, no amount of application optimization closes that gap — the data has to move closer, or the requirement has to change.

This comparison — floor vs. target — is often skipped in interviews, and naming it explicitly is a strong signal.

slides.sectionTitle: Cost as a design variable: egress, storage class, and idle compute
slides.markdown:
Three cost levers show up in almost every cloud bill, and each maps to a design decision. **Egress** — data leaving a cloud provider's network (or crossing regions) is billed per GB and adds up fast for high-traffic or video-heavy products; keeping traffic within one region, or serving from a CDN edge, avoids repeated egress charges. **Storage class** — "hot" storage (fast, expensive) vs. "cold"/archive storage (slow, cheap) — data accessed daily belongs in one tier, backups accessed once a year belong in another, and picking wrong wastes real money either way. **Idle compute** — a fleet sized for peak traffic sits mostly idle off-peak; autoscaling or serverless trades a little cold-start latency for not paying for capacity nobody's using.

Naming these three explicitly turns "it'll cost more" into a specific, defensible number.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: paying in latency vs. paying in cost
slides.markdown:
| | Fewer regions (pay in latency) | More replication/regions (pay in cost) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-region users | Slower — hit the speed-of-light floor on every request | Fast — served from a nearby replica |
| Infrastructure cost | Lower — one or two regions to run and operate | Higher — replication, cross-region egress, and duplicated infra |
| Consistency complexity | Simpler — fewer copies to keep in sync | Harder — more copies to reconcile (see CAP/PACELC) |
| Best fit | Regional products, or a latency budget that tolerates the floor | Global products where every extra 50ms measurably hurts conversion |

**How to decide:** price both sides — the cost of added regions vs. the business cost of the latency users would otherwise feel — and pick the cheaper one in the currency that actually matters here.

slides.sectionTitle: Build vs. buy under cost pressure: when a managed service is cheaper
slides.markdown:
Self-hosting a database, queue, or search cluster looks cheaper on a raw infrastructure bill than a managed equivalent — but that comparison usually omits the engineering cost of operating it: on-call for 2am failovers, patching, backups, and scaling expertise that a managed service (RDS, MSK, Elasticsearch Service) bundles into its price.

The right comparison is total cost: `(self-hosted infra cost) + (engineer-hours to operate it)` vs. `(managed service price)`. For a small team without deep operational expertise in that specific system, the managed service is very often cheaper once engineer time is priced in — even though its line-item cost looks higher.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: "solving" latency by adding replicas without pricing replication and egress
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Users in Asia are seeing high latency — let's just add a replica in a Asia-Pacific region and call it solved."

**Why it's wrong:** adding a region isn't free — it means ongoing cross-region replication traffic (often billed per GB), duplicated infrastructure cost, and new consistency questions about which region's write "wins" during a conflict. A design that fixes latency but silently triples the infra bill hasn't actually solved the problem the business cares about — it's traded one problem for a bigger, less visible one.

**Correct model:** propose the new region *and* estimate its ongoing cost (replication egress, duplicated compute), so the trade-off is a decision made with real numbers, not an unpriced assumption.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: a reference table of round-trip floors
slides.markdown:
Having a few memorized reference points turns "latency is a physical constraint" from a slogan into a number you can produce on the spot. Within one data center, round trips are typically **well under 1ms**. Within one cloud region across availability zones, expect roughly **1–2ms**. Same continent, cross-region (e.g. US-East to US-West) runs about **60–80ms** round trip. Intercontinental (US to Europe) is typically **70–100ms**; US to Asia-Pacific often **150–200ms** round trip, since the physical distance is greater still.

These are floors, not typical production numbers — real cross-region calls usually run somewhat higher once routing, processing, and queueing are added on top. But the floor is what tells you whether a target is achievable at all: a 30ms p99 requirement for a globally distributed user base is not an engineering challenge to solve with better code, it's a geography problem that requires moving data or computation physically closer to users.

Memorizing these orders of magnitude — sub-ms same-DC, low tens same-continent, high tens-to-low-hundreds intercontinental — is what lets you sanity-check a stated latency requirement in seconds during an interview, instead of discovering the conflict after designing the whole system.

slides.sectionTitle: The staff-level nuance: translating latency into revenue, not just milliseconds
slides.markdown:
Engineers naturally argue latency in milliseconds; the people approving a multi-region budget think in revenue. The senior move is converting one into the other before the conversation happens. Well-known public data points: Amazon found every **100ms** of added latency cost roughly **1% of sales**; Google found an extra **500ms** in search results cut traffic by about **20%**. These aren't universal constants for every product, but they establish the *shape* of the argument — latency has a measurable revenue slope, not just a UX-feels-nice one.

Applied concretely: if a product does $50M/year in revenue and a proposed multi-region architecture shaves 150ms off p99 for international users who represent 30% of that revenue, a rough Amazon-style estimate suggests something like `$50M x 0.30 x 1.5 x 1%` ≈ **$225K/year** in recovered revenue — a number that can be directly compared against the new region's annual cost (compute, storage, replication egress) to make the decision on the same footing instead of comparing an unquantified "user experience" against a dollar figure.

The interview-ready version: don't just say "multi-region would reduce latency for APAC users" — say what that latency reduction is plausibly worth, using the business's own revenue numbers, and let that number argue for or against the infrastructure spend.
